title: Eden Park's 52-Metre Straight Boundaries Pose India's First ODI Test in Auckland
excerpt: The Auckland ground's straight boundaries sit below the ICC minimum and survive on a pre-rule exemption, forcing both sides to rethink lengths, fields and shot selection for Wednesday's series opener.
body:
• India and New Zealand open their five-match ODI series on Wednesday, November 4 at Eden Park, Auckland, starting 3:00 p.m. local time (7:30 a.m. IST; 6:30 p.m. Pacific on Tuesday).
  • Eden Park's straight boundaries measure just 50-55 metres — below the ICC minimum of 59.43 metres — and survive only because the ground hosted internationals long before the rule existed.
  • India captain Shubman Gill called the dimensions "a bit weird," said the short straight hit is "definitely very tempting," and named field placement as the real challenge.
  • New Zealand are without Rachin Ravindra and Mark Chapman for the whole series and Devon Conway for the opener; the match will be played on a used surface.

Every touring side that comes to Auckland has to solve the same geometry problem. Eden Park, where India and New Zealand open their five-match one-day international series on Wednesday, November 4, is a rugby stadium that doubles as a cricket ground, and its rectangular shape produces boundary distances found almost nowhere else in international cricket: roughly 52 to 55 metres straight down the ground, and even less behind the wicket. Shubman Gill, who captains India in the first three ODIs, did not pretend otherwise on Tuesday. "The dimensions are a bit weird, and I think it will be a challenge for us to be able to find the right placement for the fielders," he said, in comments reported by ESPNcricinfo.

A ground that sits outside the ICC's own rule

The ICC's playing conditions for men's cricket set a minimum boundary of 65 yards (59.43 metres) and a maximum of 90 yards (82.29 metres), measured from the centre of the pitch. Eden Park's straight boundaries fall four to seven metres short of that minimum. The ground keeps its international status because it was hosting matches long before the regulations arrived — its first Test was played in 1930 — and a pitch realignment ahead of the 2011 Rugby World Cup moved the shortest boundaries dead straight, according to ESPNcricinfo. In a 2018 submission to Auckland Council, then NZC chief executive David White wrote that the ground's "small size and rectangular, football-shaped playing field continually risks compromising the integrity of cricket matches hosted there," The Sporting News reported. Square of the wicket is a different game: estimates put the square boundaries at about 65 to 68 metres, the deepest part of the ground.

"It is definitely tempting [to target the straight boundary]. Seeing the straight boundary only 50-55 meters [away]... for me, it's definitely very tempting."

— Shubman Gill, India ODI captain

What the numbers say about playing there

The data cuts against the obvious game plan. In ODIs at Eden Park since the start of 2020, fast bowlers have been hit hardest when they bowl short — an economy rate of 10.66 runs per over — because the boundaries behind the wicket are tinier still and ramps, upper-cuts and hooks carry easily. Good lengths have cost 4.21 per over and short-of-a-good-length 4.91, while even the full length, at 6.54, has been cheaper than dropping short, according to ESPNcricinfo's ball-by-ball data. Spin survives better than expected: spinners have an ODI economy rate of 5.45 at the ground since 2020 against 5.64 for seamers, though pace bowlers take wickets far more cheaply, averaging 25.98 to the spinners' 45.45. Edges fly, too — Eden Park has the second-highest not-in-control scoring rate of any ground to host at least five ODI innings since 2020. Batting first has been the safer route: three of the four ODIs there since January 2020 were won by the side batting first, with an average first-innings score of 286, according to Cricbuzz. The warning from this tour is fresh: in the fourth T20I at the same ground a few days ago, New Zealand made 259 for 7 and beat India by 87 runs.

Team news and conditions

New Zealand's absences are already substantial. Mark Chapman and Rachin Ravindra miss the entire ODI series, and Devon Conway has been ruled out of the opener after a collision in training with Matt Henry, who "seems okay," captain Mitchell Santner said; Tim Seifert comes in for Conway. Santner expects conditions to be "bouncy" and "swirly" and confirmed the match will be played on a used surface. Gill, meanwhile, flagged Auckland's cold, windy evenings — temperatures dropping to 12 to 14 degrees with wind chill — and the difficulty of chasing under lights against two new balls, feedback he said came from the T20I squad. Cricbuzz's probable India XI has Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli returning alongside Gill, with the open question being whether Kuldeep Yadav plays as the middle-overs strike option. The series continues in Wellington on November 7, Hamilton on November 10 and Mount Maunganui on November 13 and 15.
